name: Omission Bias
description: People can judge harm caused by doing something as worse than comparable or greater harm caused by not acting, even when the outcomes favor action. In practice, inaction can feel safer or less blameworthy than an active choice.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to defaults, opt-ins, consent flows, security/privacy settings, medical and safety prompts, and any decision architecture where 'leave it alone' feels morally safer than intervening even when passivity carries its own risk.
prevalence_note: Important in public-policy, health, trust, and defaults discussions, but much less commonly named in everyday product-design canon than status quo bias or loss aversion.

findings.description: A real-world mail survey of 103 parents found that those who refused or planned to refuse pertussis vaccination for their children were significantly more likely to exhibit omission bias in their reasoning (p=0.004), even after controlling for their stated beliefs about the vaccine's actual danger. Omission bias predicted a genuine, consequential health decision beyond risk perception alone -- independent, real-world confirmation of the lab-demonstrated effect, by an overlapping author team (Baron, Ritov) extending their own original 1990 paradigm into actual parental behavior.
findings.effect_size: p=0.004 (omission bias predicting vaccine refusal, controlling for risk beliefs)

findings.description: Participants were reluctant to vaccinate a hypothetical child even when the vaccine's chance of causing death was lower than the chance of death from the disease it prevented, showing a preference for harmful omission over less risky action in the vaccination scenario.
findings.source_title: Reluctance to vaccinate: Omission bias and ambiguity
